alt: Four needs (roles must be filled, by the most able, with training, and performed conscientiously) lead to unequal rewards for functionally important roles, which make people compete so the most talented win. Below, criticisms including Tumin, and Marxist and feminist views.
caption: Davis and Moore see unequal rewards as the way society gets the right people into key roles.

alt: A comparison table. Marx defines class by relationship to the means of production, splits society into bourgeoisie and proletariat, predicts polarisation and revolution, and explains acceptance through ruling class ideology. Weber defines class by market situation, sees professionals earning more, rejects polarisation and inevitable revolution, and adds status and party.
caption: Marx sees two classes heading for conflict; Weber sees a more complex, layered picture.

alt: Seven factors surround life chances: class, gender, race and ethnicity, sexuality, age, disability, and religion and belief, each with an example of how it affects a person’s chances of good health, education, a good job and housing.
caption: Seven factors in the specification shape a person’s chances of a good life.

alt: Left: what was predicted in the 1960s, privatised instrumentalism and affluent workers becoming middle class. Right: what Devine found in Luton in the late 1980s: lifestyles not as home-centred as predicted, no embourgeoisement, resentment of inherited wealth, and lost faith in the Labour Party.
caption: Devine found affluent workers kept a working-class sense of injustice: no embourgeoisement.

alt: Three measures of poverty for 1968–69. The state standard, based on benefit entitlement, gave just over 6%. Relative income gave a little over 9%. Townsend’s preferred relative deprivation measure gave more than 22%. Below, his questionnaire method and the criticism that his index may measure choice.
caption: Townsend’s relative deprivation measure found far more poverty than the official ones.

alt: Two sides. Cultural explanations: the culture of poverty and Murray’s New Right idea of an underclass created by welfare dependency. Material explanations: low wages, unemployment, poor housing, globalisation and the poverty trap. Below, functionalist, Marxist and feminist views of poverty.
caption: Is poverty caused by the values of the poor, or by lack of money and jobs?

alt: Three cards. Traditional authority rests on custom and inherited status, as in a monarchy. Charismatic authority rests on devotion to an exceptional leader. Rational-legal authority rests on shared impersonal rules, as in a bureaucracy or elected government. Below, formal and informal sources of power.
caption: Authority is accepted power, based on tradition, charisma or rules.

alt: Six numbered cards show Walby’s patriarchal structures: paid work, patriarchal relations of production, culture, sexuality, male violence and the state. Below, an arrow shows the shift from private patriarchy, direct control by fathers or husbands, to public patriarchy, where women are in public life but in low-paid, low-status jobs.
caption: Patriarchy works through six structures and has shifted from private to public.
